extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and writers who want to write epic fantasy
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for planning and writing sweeping, high‑stakes epic fantasy novels (worldbuilding, characters, magic systems, structure, and common pitfalls). Aimed at writers preparing a single novel or series entry in the epic fantasy genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with a spark
rubrics_metrics.description: Most epic fantasy stories start with a little spark—a moment, a feeling, or a 'what if' question that can expand into world‑shifting stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the spark down and ask: Where could this lead? What’s at stake? Who would this affect beyond one person? Think about ripple effects: start small and imagine how it becomes world‑shifting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your world inside and out
rubrics_metrics.description: You need to understand the rules of your world: what makes it different, the tensions shaping societies, cultures, histories, geography, and political systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider: role of magic and who can access it; how governments work; major conflicts; scarce resources and power dynamics; cultural beliefs, rituals, and taboos. You don't have to name everything, but know how these elements impact plot and characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only include what the reader needs to know
rubrics_metrics.description: When worldbuilding, include only the details necessary for the reader to understand the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save deep lore notes for appendices or your own files. Reveal lore through action, character interaction, and context rather than long info‑dumps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create complex characters with conflicting goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must feel real, flawed, and deeply human; give them clear motivations, fears, backstory, and relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about: what each character wants most, what holds them back, how their past shaped them, and who they trust or betray. Complexity and conflicting goals among characters drive emotional and plot tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist must have a personal arc tied to the epic conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should both undergo internal change and play a meaningful role in the larger, epic stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for the internal journey to mirror or contrast with the external quest so emotional payoffs feel earned and the world stakes feel personal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a consistent magic system with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If magic exists, it needs rules: who can use it, what it can/can't do, how it's learned or accessed, and what it costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define powers, costs, and constraints; consider how magic shapes society, politics, and daily life. Consistency is key—unclear rules undermine tension. Use limits and costs to create stakes and tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a story structure and stick to it
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick a structure (Hero’s Journey, Three‑Act, multiple interwoven POVs, etc.) to guide the long form of an epic fantasy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A consistent structure helps manage a marathon project. Use beat sheets, scene planners, chapter planners and timelines to map arcs and pacing across many chapters or books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure each POV/character has clear goals, stakes, obstacles, and growth
rubrics_metrics.description: Every viewpoint (or major character) should justify its presence with distinct goals and a meaningful arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid POV switches without reason; confirm each POV voice is unique and contributes to the overall narrative momentum and emotional payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with action, not exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with an event that matters (a skirmish, betrayal, coronation) to hook readers while also grounding them in the world through character perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drop readers into a scene and show the world through a character's eyes rather than narrator info‑dumps. Grounding: let sensory details and character reactions reveal social structures and magic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't info‑dump
rubrics_metrics.description: Reveal lore and world mechanics through action, dialogue, and character perceptions rather than long expository passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid front‑loading history lessons. Let characters treat extraordinary elements as normal when appropriate. Editor tip: don’t describe things your character wouldn’t notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground epic scope in emotional stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale conflict must be anchored by intimate emotional stakes so readers care about the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include moments of quiet amid chaos, create characters readers root for, and ensure emotional payoffs feel earned by showing the real cost of failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer in theme and symbolism intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Use themes (power, identity, sacrifice, faith) and symbols (objects, religious motifs, magic metaphors) to add depth and cohesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't need every symbol planned from the start, but be intentional about how magic systems, religions, or recurring images reinforce themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid info‑dumping
rubrics_metrics.description: Large blocks of lore or exposition at inappropriate times slow pacing and alienate readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sprinkle lore, integrate it into scenes, and trust readers to piece things together from context. Use appendices or external resources for encyclopedic detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly powerful characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who cannot be hurt remove tension and make conflict meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give characters vulnerability and limits—stakes only matter if loss is possible and meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid weak stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Global stakes (world ending) are meaningless without personal investment in characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie big stakes to character outcomes and relationships so the reader cares who will win or lose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage pacing to prevent exhaustion
rubrics_metrics.description: Poor pacing—too many action beats or too many information scenes—can make an epic feel exhausting or slow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance action with character moments, use scene planning and beat sheets to vary tempo across a long manuscript.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent unclear rules of magic
rubrics_metrics.description: If readers don’t understand what magic can and can’t do, tension collapses and plot solutions feel cheap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit enough about limits and costs to preserve suspense; avoid deus‑ex machina fixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep character arcs front and center
rubrics_metrics.description: Worldbuilding should not overshadow character development; characters must change over the course of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each major character experiences growth or transformation that intersects with the plot and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifts between grimdark, whimsy, or other tonal modes without a throughline can jar readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on a tonal throughline and use stylistic choices and scene placement to keep switches deliberate and earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tropes with fresh twists
rubrics_metrics.description: Common epic fantasy tropes (chosen ones, prophecies, dark lords) are acceptable but require originality to avoid cliché.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using familiar tropes, add a subversion, unique angle, or character perspective that reframes the trope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended length guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical epic fantasy novels often run long—there’s no single rule, but many fall between 100,000–150,000 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing a series, make the first book tight enough to stand alone while leaving room to expand; avoid padding to hit length.

rubrics_metrics.name: You don't need to plan the entire world before you start
rubrics_metrics.description: You need enough planning to start confidently (politics, geography, magic rules that affect the plot), but not every detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flesh out aspects that impact characters and plot first; build additional lore as you write.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple POVs are permitted but must be justified
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic fantasy often uses multiple points of view to give a panoramic view, but each POV needs a unique voice and clear reason to exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't switch heads gratuitously; ensure each POV advances plot, offers unique perspective, and has a distinct arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep track of lore and characters with systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizational systems (spreadsheets, Notion dashboards, character profiles) are essential for managing complex epics, especially across series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a consistent tracking system (character templates, timelines, beat sheets) to avoid contradictions and maintain continuity.
